span.label: null-result
span.quote: Hence the Entscheidungsproblem cannot be solved.

span.label: computability of real numbers
span.quote: The "computable" numbers may be described briefly as the real numbers whose expressions as a decimal are calculable by finite means.

span.label: mathematical-proof
span.term: mathematical-proof
span.quote: I shall enunciate a number of theorems about computability, but I shall prove only (ii) and a theorem similar to (iii).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE TERM IS INTRODUCED IN SCARE QUOTES AND GIVEN A BRIEF DESCRIPTION RATHER THAN A DEFINITION: the COMPUTABLE numbers MAY BE DESCRIBED BRIEFLY as the real numbers whose expressions as a decimal are CALCULABLE BY FINITE MEANS. The quotation marks and the word BRIEFLY both mark that the real definitional work is still to come
span.quote: The "computable" numbers may be described briefly as the real numbers whose expressions as a decimal are calculable by finite means.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE OBJECT OF STUDY IS CHOSEN FOR TECHNICAL CONVENIENCE AND THE AUTHOR SAYS SO: the subject is OSTENSIBLY the computable numbers, several other objects would be ALMOST EQUALLY EASY to treat, THE FUNDAMENTAL PROBLEMS INVOLVED ARE THE SAME IN EACH CASE - and the numbers were chosen FOR EXPLICIT TREATMENT AS INVOLVING THE LEAST CUMBROUS TECHNIQUE. What the paper is about is a presentational decision
span.quote: Although the subject of this paper is ostensibly the computable numbers. it is almost equally easy to define and investigate computable functions of an integral variable or a real or computable variable, computable predicates, and so forth. The fundamental problems involved are, however, the same in each case, and I have chosen the computable numbers for explicit treatment as involving the least cumbrous technique.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE DEFINITION IS OFFERED IN THE FIRST PERSON POSSESSIVE: ACCORDING TO MY DEFINITION, a number is computable IF ITS DECIMAL CAN BE WRITTEN DOWN BY A MACHINE. The criterion is a capability of a device, and the sentence marks that this is one definition among possible others
span.quote: According to my definition, a number is computable if its decimal can be written down by a machine.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE ADEQUACY OF THE DEFINITION TO THE INFORMAL NOTION IS ANNOUNCED AS SOMETHING TO BE ARGUED IN ITS OWN SECTIONS: two sections are given over to ARGUMENTS WITH THE INTENTION OF SHOWING that the computable numbers INCLUDE ALL NUMBERS WHICH COULD NATURALLY BE REGARDED AS COMPUTABLE - so the match between the formal class and the natural one is itself a claim requiring support
span.quote: In §§ 9, 10 I give some arguments with the intention of showing that the computable numbers include all numbers which could naturally be regarded as computable.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: TWO NEIGHBOURING TERMS ARE SEPARATED BY A COUNTEREXAMPLE RATHER THAN BY ARGUMENT: the computable numbers DO NOT include all DEFINABLE numbers, AND AN EXAMPLE IS GIVEN of a definable number which is not computable. The boundary between the two words is established by exhibiting one object that falls on the far side of it
span.quote: The computable numbers do not, however, include all definable numbers, and an example is given of a definable number which is not computable.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: ANOTHER AUTHOR'S TERM IS RECORDED AS EQUIVALENT AND VERY DIFFERENTLY DEFINED: Church has introduced an idea of EFFECTIVE CALCULABILITY, WHICH IS EQUIVALENT TO MY COMPUTABILITY, BUT IS VERY DIFFERENTLY DEFINED - and the PROOF of the equivalence is deferred to an appendix. Two vocabularies, one extension, and the identity is a theorem rather than a convention
span.quote: In a recent paper Alonzo Church f has introduced an idea of "effective calculability", which is equivalent to my "computability", but is very differently defined.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE CENTRAL ADMISSION, AND IT IS THIS PROJECT'S PROBLEM STATED IN 1936: NO ATTEMPT HAS YET BEEN MADE to show that the COMPUTABLE numbers include all numbers WHICH WOULD NATURALLY BE REGARDED AS COMPUTABLE, and ALL ARGUMENTS WHICH CAN BE GIVEN ARE BOUND TO BE, FUNDAMENTALLY, APPEALS TO INTUITION, AND FOR THIS REASON RATHER UNSATISFACTORY MATHEMATICALLY. Whether a formalism captures the notion it was built for cannot be proved, only argued - said by the person who built the formalism
span.quote: No attempt has yet been made to show that the " computable " numbers include all numbers which would naturally be regarded as computable. Al I arguments which can be given are bound to be, fundamentally, appeals to intuition, and for this reason rather unsatisfactory mathematically.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE QUESTION BEHIND THE DEFINITION IS NAMED, AND IT IS NOT A MATHEMATICAL QUESTION: THE REAL QUESTION AT ISSUE IS WHAT ARE THE POSSIBLE PROCESSES WHICH CAN BE CARRIED OUT IN COMPUTING A NUMBER. The formal apparatus is answerable to a claim about what can be done, not about what follows from axioms
span.quote: The real question at issue is " What are the possible processes which can be carried out in computing a number?"

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A TAXONOMY OF WAYS TO ARGUE THAT A DEFINITION CAPTURES ITS CONCEPT, WITH A CONDITION ON THE SECOND: (a) A DIRECT APPEAL TO INTUITION; (b) A PROOF OF THE EQUIVALENCE OF TWO DEFINITIONS - IN CASE THE NEW DEFINITION HAS A GREATER INTUITIVE APPEAL; (c) GIVING EXAMPLES OF LARGE CLASSES of numbers which are computable. **An equivalence proof is evidence for adequacy only if one of the two definitions is the more intuitive** - otherwise it moves the problem rather than solving it
span.quote: The arguments which I shall use are of three kinds. (a) A direct appeal to intuition. (6) A proof of the equivalence of two definitions (in case the new definition has a greater intuitive appeal). (c) Giving examples of large classes of numbers which are computable.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A FEATURE OF THE APPARATUS IS DECLARED INESSENTIAL BY AN APPEAL TO THE READER'S ASSENT: the two-dimensional character of the paper IS SOMETIMES USED in elementary arithmetic, but SUCH A USE IS ALWAYS AVOIDABLE, and - I THINK THAT IT WILL BE AGREED - it is NO ESSENTIAL of computation. The idealisation is argued for rather than assumed, and the argument offered is that the reader will agree
span.quote: In elementary arithmetic the two-dimensional character of the paper is sometimes used. But such a use is always avoidable, and I think that it will be agreed that the two-dimensional character of paper is no essential

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A RESTRICTION IS JUSTIFIED BY THE INDISCRIMINABILITY THAT WOULD FOLLOW WITHOUT IT, AND THEN MINIMISED: if an infinity of symbols were allowed there would be SYMBOLS DIFFERING TO AN ARBITRARILY SMALL EXTENT - and the effect of the restriction IS NOT VERY SERIOUS, because SEQUENCES of symbols can always be used in place of single ones. The bound is defended by what could not be told apart
span.quote: I shall also suppose that the number of symbols which may be printed is finite. If we were to allow an infinity of symbols, then there would be symbols differing to an arbitrarily small extent j. The effect of this restriction of the number of symbols is not very serious. It is always possible to use sequences of symbols in the place of single symbols.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE SAME ARGUMENT IS APPLIED TO THE MIND, AND ITS FORM IS EXPLICITLY REUSED: the number of STATES OF MIND which need be taken into account is finite, THE REASONS FOR THIS ARE OF THE SAME CHARACTER as those restricting the symbols, because an infinity of states of mind would include some ARBITRARILY CLOSE that WILL BE CONFUSED - and again the restriction DOES NOT SERIOUSLY AFFECT COMPUTATION, since complicated states can be traded for more symbols on the tape
span.quote: We will also suppose that the number of states of mind which need be taken into account is finite. The reasons for this are of the same character as those which restrict the number of symbols. If we admitted an infinity of states of mind, some of them will be '' arbitrarily close " and will be confused. Again, the restriction is not one which seriously affects computation, since the use of more complicated states of mind can be avoided by writing more symbols on the tape.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE ATOM OF THE ANALYSIS IS DEFINED BY THE LIMITS OF IMAGINATION: the operations are split into SIMPLE OPERATIONS WHICH ARE SO ELEMENTARY THAT IT IS NOT EASY TO IMAGINE THEM FURTHER DIVIDED. What counts as indivisible is fixed by what cannot readily be pictured as divided, not by a property of the operations
span.quote: Let us imagine the operations performed by the computer to be split up into "simple operations" which are so elementary that it is not easy to imagine them further divided.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AN EMPIRICAL CLAIM ABOUT READING IS ADMITTED INTO A MATHEMATICAL ARGUMENT AND MARKED AS SUCH: compound symbols, if too lengthy, CANNOT BE OBSERVED AT ONE GLANCE - THIS IS IN ACCORDANCE WITH EXPERIENCE - and the demonstration offered is that WE CANNOT TELL AT A GLANCE whether two long strings of nines are the same. A fact about human perception is doing load-bearing work in a proof about computability
span.quote: The differences from our point of view between the single and compound symbols is that the compound symbols, if they are too lengthy, cannot be observed at one glance. This is in accordance with experience. We cannot tell at a glance whether 9999999999999999 and 999999999999999 are the same.

span.label: The case that the machine definition captures everything intuitively computable can only be argued by appeal to intuition, which the author calls mathematically unsatisfactory.
span.quote: Al I arguments which can be given are bound to be, fundamentally, appeals to intuition, and for this reason rather unsatisfactory mathematically.

span.label: A consistency proof required for the recursion result is not supplied.
span.quote: I shall not give the proof of consistency of %n.

span.label: Classical analysis does not carry over unchanged: a computable bounded increasing sequence of computable numbers need not have a computable limit.
span.quote: Owing to this restriction of Dedekind's theorem, we cannot say that a computable bounded increasing sequence of computable numbers has a computable limit.

span.label: The computable numbers are strictly narrower than the definable numbers.
span.quote: The computable numbers do not, however, include all definable numbers, and an example is given of a definable number which is not computable.

span.label: The definition of the central term is justified by an empirical claim about human beings, and the justification is postponed.
span.quote: No real attempt will be made to justify the definitions given until we reach § 9. For the present I shall only say that the justification lies in the fact that the human memory is necessarily limited

span.label: The class defined does not exhaust the numbers that can be named, and the paper supplies a counterexample.
span.quote: The computable numbers do not, however, include all definable numbers, and an example is given of a definable number which is not computable

span.label: There is no procedure that decides the property the whole construction turns on.
span.quote: we have no general process for doing this in a finite number of steps. In fact, by applying the diagonal process argument correctly, we can show that there cannot be any such general process

span.label: The translation between the paper's informal vocabulary and its machine vocabulary is valid only if the central definition is, and the paper says so in the same breath.
span.quote: The expression "there is a general process for determining..." has been used throughout this section as equivalent to "there is a machine which will determine ... ". This usage can be justified if and only if we can justify our definition of "computable"

span.label: my “computability” → the intuitive notion of an effectively calculable number
span.note: THREE PAPERS, THREE DIFFERENT VERDICTS ON WHETHER A FORMALISM CAN BE SHOWN TO CAPTURE THE INFORMAL NOTION IT REPLACES - and no type in the vocabulary can express a disagreement about what KIND OF CLAIM something is. This paper ARGUES the identification rather than proving it, and enumerates the three kinds of argument available: a direct appeal to intuition, a proof of the equivalence of two definitions where the new one has greater intuitive appeal, and examples of large classes of computable numbers. shor1997-factoring says the same identification cannot be made a theorem without weakening it; tkacik2016-information-living reports a theorem that did make a vague notion precise. **`same-as` and `distinct-from` are both false here**: the three are not making one claim or two, they are ruling differently on whether the identification is the sort of thing a proof can settle. All eight edge types assert that a relation holds between two concepts. Recorded per record, each row quoting only its own paper; the cross-paper half is this paraphrase, checkable by opening the other two. Q-709, and the third case for Q-632 - which by the rule that one is an observation and three make a proposal is the point at which the gap should be put to Shir.
span.quote: The arguments which I shall use are of three kinds. (a) A direct appeal to intuition. (6) A proof of the equivalence of two definitions (in case the new definition has a greater intuitive appeal). (c) Giving examples of large classes of numbers which are computable.

span.label: circular and circle-free - THE DISTINCTION THE FIELD LATER RENAMED 'HALTING', WITH THE POLES SWAPPED IN VALUE: a machine is circular if it never writes more than finitely many symbols of the first kind, and circle-free otherwise, so the machine that runs forever is the SUCCESSFUL one here and the word 'halting' names the failure case as though it were the subject
span.quote: If a computing machine never writes down more than a finite number of symbols of the first kind, it will be called circular. Otherwise it is said to be circle-free

span.label: 'a general process for determining' - DECLARED EQUIVALENT TO 'a machine which will determine': the paper states its own translation rule between informal and machine vocabulary, says it holds throughout the section, and makes it conditional on the definition of computable being justified
span.quote: The expression "there is a general process for determining..." has been used throughout this section as equivalent to "there is a machine which will determine ... ". This usage can be justified if and only if we can justify our definition of "computable"

span.label: the computer - A HUMAN BEING: throughout the argument of section 9 'the computer' is a person observing symbols and holding a state of mind, with a bound on how many squares he can observe at once; the word now denotes the machine that was built to replace him
span.quote: The behaviour of the computer at any moment is determined by the symbols which he is observing, and his " state of mind " at that moment. We may suppose that there is a bound B to the number of symbols or squares which the computer can observe at one moment

span.label: computable - AS WRITABLE-DOWN-BY-A-MACHINE: the definition is stated in terms of a machine producing the decimal, not in terms of a formula or a rule
span.quote: According to my definition, a number is computable if its decimal can be written down by a machine

span.label: A number is computable if its decimal can be written down by a machine operating by finite means; Turing defines such machines (tape, m-configurations, scanned symbols) capturing everything naturally regarded as computable.
span.quote: According to my definition, a number is computable if its decimal can be written down by a machine.

span.label: A single UNIVERSAL computing machine can compute any computable sequence — the basis for resolving the Entscheidungsproblem, since some definable numbers are provably not computable.
span.quote: It is possible to invent a single machine which can be used to compute any computable sequence.
